newsitem.title: KENYA: Opposition welcomes IMF move to halt loan to Kenya.
newsitem.headline: Opposition welcomes IMF move to halt loan to Kenya.

text.p: Kenya's opposition hailed on Friday a decision by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to halt a key loan package and said it would hit the Kenyan shilling and investment.

"I'm very pleased the IMF has finally recognised the enormous problem of governance in this country," said Richard Leakey, secretary-general of the unregistered Safina party, which campaigned for political reforms and against corruption.
"We have been asking the IMF for a very long time to take this measure and obviously it will hit a lot of projects," he told Reuters. "Corruption was absolutely central to the IMF decision."
"You are going to see the (Kenyan) shilling lose value very rapidly and it will have a lot of knock-on effects -- on foreign investment for instance," Leakey said before Nairobi markets opened.

"But I sincerely hope the authorities in this country will take the appropriate response in terms of starting the process of reforms," he added. "The government attempts to constantly window dress have finally been seen through by the IMF."

The IMF said on Thursday a $205 million three-year loan, offered under the IMF's Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility, would be allowed to lapse because the Kenyan government's response to a July 24 deadline for change had been inadequate.
The IMF turned down a request from the government of President Daniel arap Moi for more time to try to take measures to meet IMF concerns about corruption and demands for reform of the energy sector.
An opposition-backed alliance campaigning for political reforms before this year's general election has called for a nationwide general strike on August 8 to put the government under more pressure.

In an editorial written before the IMF decision was announced in Washington, the independent Daily Nation newspaper said on Friday the IMF clearly believed the government was reluctant to punish corruption.

"The perception in the donor community is that the government has played hide and seek with the IMF over the Goldenberg scam," said the Nation, referring to a multi-million-dollar financial scandal involving Goldenberg International.
"But that is just one scam. Year in and year out, parliament's public accounts committee and the auditor-general bring out reports that point to massive abuse and misuse of public funds," it said.

"We think the reason why there is reluctance to punish corruption in government is that it is highly placed people who are involved...Such highly placed people are involved in corruption because they know they will go scott-free," it said.
The IMF has focused on the Goldenberg scandal to illustrate how Kenyan authorities are reluctant to punish corruption.
Goldenberg International was paid about $100 million by the government in 1992 under an scheme for gold and diamond exports. Kenya produces very little gold and no diamonds.
The IMF delayed releasing the $36 million ESAF tranche after Kenya's high court decided on June 20 to end the prosecution of a businessman and former officials implicated in the scandal.
Authorities however have charged the businessman and former officials again.
The opposition had cited alleged links to powerful Kenyan politicians as the main reason the prosecution was dropped.
